report:
Based on this research, here is my assessment:

## Conclusion: The claim is **not supported** — capsaicin does not treat breast cancer in humans.

**What the evidence actually shows:**

1. **Preclinical (lab/animal) promise exists, but is preliminary.** Multiple in-vitro studies show capsaicin inhibits proliferation and induces apoptosis in human breast cancer cell lines (e.g., MCF-7, MDA-MB-231) via pathways like NF-κB/FBI-1 and CDK8/PI3K/Wnt-β-catenin (https://www.dovepress.com/capsaicin-inhibits-proliferation-and-induces-apoptosis-in-breast-cance-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DDDT). These are cell-culture experiments, not human treatment data.

2. **No human clinical trials demonstrate capsaicin treats breast cancer.** A comprehensive review states plainly that "the clinical value of per os capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative," even though animal models show some anti-tumor afferent nerve effects (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). Claims of a "University of Pittsburgh clinical trial" curing cancer are not substantiated by primary literature and appear to conflate lab studies with clinical trials (https://medshun.com/article/capsaicin-breast-cancer-treatment).

3. **Some evidence points the opposite direction — capsaicin may promote cancer progression.** Animal studies show capsaicin-induced denervation of sensory neurons can *promote* mammary tumor metastasis to lung and heart, and low-dose capsaicin has been shown to promote colorectal cancer metastasis via ROS/Akt/mTOR/STAT3 pathways (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/). This is a serious complicating factor.

4. **Fact-checkers have addressed viral claims directly.** Snopes concluded capsaicin has anticancer properties in lab settings, but its use as actual cancer therapy in humans "is far from certain," citing major delivery and dosing challenges (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).

**Bottom line:** Capsaicin is a legitimate research subject for cancer chemoprevention, with mixed and sometimes contradictory preclinical findings (both tumor-suppressing and tumor-promoting effects depending on model/dose). No credible human clinical trial evidence supports capsaicin as a breast cancer treatment. Patients should not substitute capsaicin for established therapies.
